Equipment

My rifles

Tap a rifle to shoot it; its bullet, sight and zero are edited inside. A rifle keeps the bullet, muzzle velocity, twist, sight height, zero, reticle and turret — not the weather or the distances, which change every outing. Edits are not written back until you choose Update from its ⋯ menu, so a rifle you have changed says “modified” until then. The same menu renames it, shares it on the public list and deletes it.

Barrel and zero

What it shoots, and what you look through

Zeroing conditions

Your zero was set on one particular day. Press the button on that day and its weather is kept with the rifle; changing the zero range keeps it too, while nothing has been recorded yet. Turn the correction on and the scope angle is solved under those conditions while the bullet flies through today's air — which is what actually happens. Leave it off and the solver assumes you zeroed in the conditions you are shooting in now.

A scope sets its reticle, its click value and, when the table reads MIL or MOA, the unit of its turrets. The sight height stays: it is the rifle's mount. Each reticle is drawn from its maker's published subtension drawing.

Saved

The shared list

What you save goes to a public list.

Bullets, sights and rifles you save or share are sent to a list everyone using this page can see and load, and anyone can add to it. Do not put anything in a name you would not publish. Deleting one of yours removes it from your list; the copy already sent stays on the shared list for others. Somebody else's cannot be deleted, only hidden from yours.

Environment

Where you are

It runs only when pressed. It asks the browser for your position, then sends those coordinates to the Open-Meteo public API, which returns temperature, station pressure, humidity, wind and the height of the ground there. If the browser cannot give a position, the latitude and longitude already in the fields are used instead, so typing them in is always a way through. The wind is a 10 m forecast for the area, not what your flags are doing.

Atmosphere

Station pressure is what a Kestrel reads — not the altimeter setting corrected to sea level. Positive shot angle is uphill. Latitude and azimuth drive the Coriolis term.

Wind

Drag the dial, or use the arrow keys. The clock is relative to your shot: 12 o'clock blows from the target into your face, 3 o'clock from your right.

90° 3 o'clock

Output

A turret factor other than 1.000 scales the clicks you dial. Set it only if you have measured your scope's tracking on a tall target: a scope that moves 9.7 MIL when you dial 10.0 has a factor of 10.0 / 9.7 = 1.031.

Shot log

Every logged shot stores the prediction, what you actually dialled, and the complete setup that produced it — bullet, rifle, zero, atmosphere and wind. From 1.9.0 a shot is logged as a hit and where it landed is not asked. It is recorded to check whether the model is realistic; it never feeds back into the solver, because a prediction corrected by the last observation is no longer an independent test of anything.

Ported from the PyBallisticsV2 solver (Python + NumPy), validated cell-by-cell against it across 22 configurations. The canonical M852 case reproduces −1357.3097 cm of drop at 1000 m. Aerodynamic coefficients: BRL MR-3733 (McCoy); standard drag functions G7/G1 per McCoy. Weather by Open-Meteo. Academic tool — verify against your own data before trusting a solution.
